name: Milk Stout
title: Milk Stout: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Milk stout explained: why lactose keeps it sweet, how it differs from oatmeal and dry stout, and which Indian desserts suit it.
tagline: A soft, sweet stout that tastes like coffee with milk and sugar.
tastes:
Milk stout gets its sweetness from lactose, the sugar in milk. Brewer's yeast cannot ferment lactose, so whatever goes into the kettle stays in the beer as sweetness and body. English brewers sold it in the early twentieth century as a nourishing drink, with advertising that would never pass today, and it was a working class staple in Britain for decades.

The flavour is roast coffee and chocolate, softened by that unfermentable sugar into something like a sweetened latte or a chocolate milk for grown ups. Bitterness is low, carbonation is gentle and the strength is modest, usually 3 to 6 percent. The roast stops it from tasting like dessert in a glass.

Many modern versions add vanilla, coffee or cocoa nibs. That is fine, but a plain milk stout should still taste balanced. One practical note: lactose is a dairy sugar, so a milk stout is not suitable for vegans or anyone avoiding dairy.

profile.look: Very dark brown to black, opaque, with a creamy tan head of good retention.
profile.aroma_flavour: Sweetened coffee, milk chocolate and caramel, with gentle roast. Low hop aroma. Sweetness is obvious but should not be sticky.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium to full body, smooth and creamy from the lactose. Low to moderate carbonation and a sweet, soft finish.
profile.ingredients: Pale ale malt with roasted barley, chocolate and crystal malts. Lactose added in the boil, usually 5 to 10 percent of fermentables. English hops for modest bitterness. English ale yeast.

in_india: Indians grew up on sweet milky chai and filter coffee, so milk stout tends to make sense on the first sip even to people who say they do not like dark beer. Brewpubs pour it more often than bottlers, frequently with vanilla or coffee. It holds up well in a warm supply chain, since roast and lactose are stable. Serve it cool, not frozen, and pair it with dessert. Remember to tell guests it contains dairy.

pairings.why: The beer's sweetness soothes the chilli and tamarind, and its roast suits the fried bhatura.
Ghee fried bread and cardamom milk meet the latte sweetness of the stout and taste even richer.
The nutty ghee sweetness lines up with the milk chocolate and caramel notes.
Coconut and roasted spice meet roast malt, and the residual sweetness takes the edge off the heat.
